7.text: A number of specimens of ivory armor, chiefly from the American side

8.text: of Bering Sea, are in the possession of the United States National Museum

9.text: in Washington, but all of these are incomplete. Those represented in the

10.text: valuable paper by Walter Hough on primitive American armor come respectively

11.text: from Cape Prince of Wales and Diomede Island.² Apparently there is no

12.text: difference between them and the specimens brought from the Asiatic shore.

13.text: Mr. Hough mentions, besides, four armor-plates of fossil ivory from Cape

14.text: Wañqarêˊman, on the Arctic shore; also nine iron plates found together with

15.text: the ivory armor in a bog at Cape Prince of Wales. According to a com-

16.text: munication of Capt. E. P. Herendeen, quoted by Mr. Hough,³ the Chukchee

17.text: of Plover Bay, i. e., probably the Aiˊwan Eskimo, wore a cuirass made of

18.text: long strips of baleen; but from Capt. Herendeen’s words it is not clear

19.text: whether he saw this kind of armor or only repeats the words of the natives.

31.text: A stiff hide head-protector is fastened above the armor. It evidently

32.text: served to protect the neck from behind and from both sides. Mr. Hough

33.text: compares it to the neck-fender of the Kingsmill Island⁵ armor.

34.text: The specimen of hide armor now in St. Petersburg is made of ground-

35.text: seal skin. According to Mr. Hough, the armor in Washington is made of

36.text: sea-lion hide; but I should think rather that it also is made of ground-seal

37.text: skin, because sea-lions are scarce near the shores of the Chukchee Peninsula.
